title: Qualcomm Beats Estimates as Phones Shrink and Data Center Bet Grows
excerpt: Fiscal Q4 revenue rose 8% to $11.27 billion and non-GAAP EPS hit $3.00, but a $5.7 billion tax charge cut GAAP profit and handset revenue fell 2%.
body:
• Qualcomm's fiscal Q4 2026 revenue rose 8% year over year to $11.27 billion, beating the $10.77 billion analysts expected; non-GAAP earnings were $3.00 per share against $2.88 expected.
  • GAAP profit was hit by a one-time $5.7 billion tax charge, cutting net income to $1.09 billion, or $1.01 per share.
  • Handset chip revenue fell 2% to $6.63 billion, while automotive jumped 36% to $1.02 billion and IoT rose 10% to $2.17 billion.
  • The growth bet is AI data centers: the new AI200 and AI250 inference accelerators enter production in fiscal 2028, with Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN as the first named deployment customer.

Qualcomm beat Wall Street's expectations for its fiscal fourth quarter, reporting revenue of $11.27 billion, up 8% from a year earlier, and non-GAAP earnings of $3.00 per share. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected $10.77 billion in revenue and $2.88 per share, according to CNBC. The chipmaker's GAAP numbers looked far weaker — net income of $1.09 billion, or $1.01 per share, against $3.03 a year earlier — because of a one-time, non-cash $5.7 billion charge tied to US tax reform and the valuation of deferred tax assets, a hit the company had flagged in advance.

The phone business is shrinking; everything else is growing

Qualcomm's chip division, QCT, delivered $9.82 billion of the quarter's revenue. Handsets remain the largest piece at $6.63 billion, but that fell 2% year over year, and Apple — long one of Qualcomm's biggest modem customers — is moving to its own in-house modems. The growth came from the diversification lines Qualcomm has spent years building: automotive revenue rose 36% to $1.02 billion, and Internet of Things revenue rose 10% to $2.17 billion. Licensing, the company's high-margin QTL arm, contributed $1.32 billion.

https://x.com/Qualcomm/status/2118109709295104194

Full-year fiscal 2026 revenue reached $44.28 billion, up 6%, with non-GAAP earnings of $12.03 per share. For the current quarter, Qualcomm guided to revenue of $12.2 billion to $13.0 billion and non-GAAP earnings of $3.33 to $3.49 per share.

The data center bet

The strategic story is Qualcomm's push into AI data centers, a market Nvidia dominates. Its AI200 and AI250 accelerators are inference chips — hardware that runs trained AI models rather than training them — paired with next-generation CPUs, a new software stack and rack-scale systems. Saudi Arabia's HUMAIN is the first named deployment customer, targeting 200 megawatts from 2026. The timeline is long: the AI200 enters production in the first quarter of fiscal 2028 and the AI250 in the third quarter, so data center revenue is a 2027-and-beyond story, not a current one. Qualcomm's Dragonfly platform, aimed at industrial, robotics and edge-AI uses, is sampling to lead customers, with product shipments beginning in the coming months.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DeQA_2Wl7OM/

"We are extending our leadership in on-device AI and intelligent computing into the data center — unlocking a $150B market opportunity."

— Qualcomm, fiscal Q4 2026 earnings infographic

CEO Cristiano Amon framed the shift as a multi-year transformation. "Qualcomm is undergoing a profound transformation from a wireless connectivity company to a connected computing leader for the age of AI," he said, pointing to growth targets of more than $20 billion in automotive and IoT revenue by fiscal 2029 and over $9 billion in data center revenue by fiscal 2031.

What to watch

The gap in the story is timing and competition. Qualcomm's data center silicon does not reach production until fiscal 2028, into a market where Nvidia and a crowd of custom-silicon rivals are already shipping. Meanwhile the handset business that funds the transition is shrinking, squeezed by Apple's in-house modems and weak smartphone demand. The full release is on GlobeNewswire. For now, investors are being asked to value Qualcomm on the businesses it is building — automotive, IoT and eventually data centers — rather than the phone franchise that built it.
